title: English Vocabulary 3 · Units 27–28
description: Curated B2 clothing vocabulary, garment alterations, fit and fabric descriptions, symptoms, illness expressions and medical treatment patterns.
sourceNotice: Prepared from the user-supplied book for personal study. Vocabulary targets follow source topics and exercise vocabulary; all teaching examples and notes are newly written, and original exercises, extended passages and illustrations are not reproduced.

audit.scope: Illustrated study pages, tables, grammar and common-mistake notes, exercise prompts and relevant answer-key entries checked for vocabulary, contrasts and collocations.
audit.pronunciation: Selected broad British IPA for checked words and short expressions; longer or uncertain pronunciations omit IPA rather than supply an unverified transcription.
audit.languagePolicy: English in all fields except Brazilian Portuguese glosses under pt.
audit.reviewMethod: Manual comparison of source study pages, illustrations, exercises and answer key; lexical and example review; offline schema, ID and audio-target validation. Live VocabLab UI import and browser TTS/speech recognition were not tested.
audit.limitations: No bundled recordings. Browser text-to-speech, automatic pronunciation assessment and runtime application import were not exercised.

units.title: Unit 27 — Clothes
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 27. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.
learningObjectives: Describe garments and less familiar parts of clothing, including fastenings and shoe parts.
Distinguish clothing verbs and patterns such as try on, dress up, take in, take up, suit, match and fit.
Describe fit, necklines, sleeves, materials and patterns using natural adjective–noun collocations.
Use plural clothing nouns with a pair of and discuss clothing appearance, disguises and inside-out garments.

items.example: After the late flight, I went straight home and changed into my pyjamas.
items.note: British spelling pyjamas; American English often uses pajamas. The noun is plural in form.

items.example: She wore a thick hoodie under her jacket.
items.note: An informal top with a hood, usually made of sweatshirt fabric.

items.example: She packed a bikini for the beach holiday.
items.note: A two-piece swimsuit.

items.example: The shop sells sports bras in different sizes.
items.note: A shortened form of brassiere; a normal everyday word.

items.example: Always wear a helmet when riding a motorbike.
items.note: Protective headgear used for cycling, motorcycling and some sports.

items.example: He changed into slippers as soon as he came indoors.
items.note: Soft indoor footwear; usually used in the plural.

items.example: The security guard wore an identification badge on her jacket.
items.note: A small symbol or sign attached to clothing; not the same as a belt buckle.

items.example: I had to loosen my belt after lunch.
items.note: A strip worn round the waist to hold clothing in place.

items.example: His shirt collar was slightly creased.
items.note: The part of a shirt or coat around the neck.

items.example: The zip on my jacket got stuck halfway up.
items.note: British English zip; American English commonly zipper.

items.example: She folded back the cuffs of her shirt.
items.note: The finished end of a sleeve around the wrist.

items.example: There is a small tear in the left sleeve.
items.note: A part of a garment that covers all or part of an arm.

items.example: He pulled up his hood when it began to rain.
items.note: A fabric covering attached to clothing that goes over the head.

items.example: The hem of the skirt needs repairing.
items.note: The sewn or folded edge at the bottom of a garment.

items.example: The metal buckle on my belt has broken.
items.note: A fastener often used on belts or shoes.

items.example: Tie your laces before you go down the stairs.
items.note: Shoe laces are strings used to fasten footwear; usually plural in this context.

items.example: The sole of this boot is starting to come away.
items.note: The bottom part of a shoe that touches the ground; not the heel.

items.example: One heel broke as she was crossing the street.
items.note: Can refer to the back or raised part of footwear; also a body part.

items.example: I bought a pair of trousers for the conference.
items.note: Trousers is plural-only in this meaning: these trousers are, or a pair of trousers is.

items.example: He needs a new pair of jeans for the trip.
items.note: Use a pair of with one item; jeans takes a plural verb when used alone.

items.example: I always take a pair of shorts when I go hiking.
items.note: Shorts is plural-only when referring to this garment.

items.example: She bought a pair of tights to wear with the dress.
items.note: British tights means a close-fitting garment covering legs and waist; American pantyhose in some contexts.

items.pt: uma cueca; uma peça de roupa íntima inferior
items.example: He packed three pairs of underpants for the weekend.
items.note: Underpants is plural-only; use pairs to count individual garments.

items.example: Could I try on this jacket before buying it?
items.note: Separable phrasal verb: try it on, not try on it.

items.example: We usually dress up for the annual awards dinner.
items.note: In the source this means wear smart or special clothes; it can also mean wear a costume.

items.pt: alargar uma roupa soltando a costura
items.example: A tailor can let out the waist of these trousers.
items.note: A clothing alteration that makes a garment wider or looser.

items.pt: alongar uma roupa descendo a bainha
items.example: We could let down the hem to make the skirt longer.
items.note: Clothing sense: lengthen a garment by releasing folded fabric at the hem.

items.example: The dress is too loose, so I'll have it taken in.
items.note: Clothing sense: make a garment narrower, often at the waist or sides.

items.pt: encurtar uma roupa fazendo a bainha
items.example: These trousers are too long and need taking up.
items.note: Clothing sense: shorten trousers, skirts or dresses at the hem.

items.pt: tirar uma roupa para vestir outra
items.example: He changed out of his work clothes after getting home.
items.note: Pattern: change out of clothes and into other clothes.

items.pt: trocar de roupa e vestir outra
items.example: She changed into a dry T-shirt after the rain.
items.note: Pattern: change into + clothes or uniform.

items.pt: combinar com a aparência de alguém; cair bem
items.example: That warm shade of green really suits you.
items.note: Clothing sense: look attractive on a person; not the same as fit or match.

items.example: The red scarf matches her gloves.
items.note: Match describes items or colours that look alike or go well together.

items.example: These shoes don't fit my feet properly.
items.note: Fit is about size or shape, not whether a colour looks attractive on someone.

items.pt: crescer e deixar de caber em uma roupa
items.example: My nephew has already grown out of his winter coat.
items.note: Often means becoming too big for clothes; also has an unrelated figurative sense.

items.example: She prefers baggy trousers for travelling.
items.note: Loose-fitting, often with excess fabric; can be an intentional style.

items.example: He wore a close-fitting top under his coat.
items.note: Fits closely against the body; contrasts with baggy.

items.example: My old jacket feels too tight across the shoulders.
items.note: Can mean uncomfortably narrow or closely fitted.

items.example: The waistband is so loose that the skirt keeps slipping.
items.note: Can describe a garment that is too large or deliberately relaxed.

items.example: Bring a long-sleeved shirt in case it gets cold.
items.note: Compound adjective before a noun: a long-sleeved shirt.

items.example: A sleeveless dress is comfortable in hot weather.
items.note: Made without sleeves.

items.example: He chose a V-neck jumper rather than a round-neck one.
items.note: Describes the shape of a neckline; often used before a clothing noun.

items.example: The shop sells round-neck cotton T-shirts.
items.note: An adjective describing a rounded neckline.

items.example: The denim jacket is thick enough for a cool evening.
items.note: A sturdy fabric widely used for jeans and jackets.

items.example: She wore a woollen scarf on the cold morning.
items.note: British spelling woollen; American woolen; describes material made from wool.

items.example: Rain can damage suede shoes if they are not protected.
items.note: A type of leather with a soft, slightly rough surface.

items.example: He wanted a plain white shirt without a pattern.
items.note: For fabric or clothes, plain means not patterned or decorated.

items.example: She wore a striped blouse with dark trousers.
items.note: A pattern of parallel lines; distinguish from checked.

items.example: A checked shirt works well with plain jeans.
items.note: A pattern made from crossing lines that form squares.

items.example: She bought a flowery summer dress.
items.note: Describes a fabric printed with flowers.

items.example: The dancer wore a traditional tartan skirt.
items.note: A distinctive crossed-stripe pattern, often associated with Scottish dress.

items.example: He arrived in a dark pinstriped suit.
items.note: Fine, narrow vertical lines, especially on formal suits.

items.example: The spotted blouse has tiny white dots.
items.note: A spotted pattern contains small circular marks or dots.

items.example: She looked elegant in a simple black dress.
items.note: Stylish and attractive in a refined way.

items.example: He was dressed casually for the meeting with friends.
items.note: An adverbial expression meaning wearing comfortable informal clothes.

items.example: She avoids spending too much on designer sunglasses.
items.note: Designer means produced or marketed by a well-known fashion designer.

items.example: The dancers wore their national costume during the festival.
items.note: Traditional clothing associated with a country or culture.

items.example: His sweatshirt was inside out, with the seams showing.
items.note: Used when the inner surface of clothing faces outwards.

items.example: Check the label before washing the coat.
items.note: A tag providing brand, size or care information; can also be used figuratively.

items.example: The actor wore a mask to hide his face.
items.note: Here it can be part of a disguise.

items.example: The costume served as a convincing disguise.
items.note: Something that changes a person's appearance to conceal their identity.

items.pt: cardigã; casaco de malha aberto na frente
items.example: She put on a cardigan when the room became chilly.
items.note: A knitted top that opens down the front; accepted in the answer key.

items.example: One of the buttons came off his coat.
items.note: The answer key uses buttons as something to sew on; singular form is used as the target.

items.example: Please do up your laces before you go outside.
items.note: Do up means fasten or tie in this context; another useful verb is tie.

items.example: I turned my pockets inside out looking for the missing ticket.
items.note: In the illustrated exercise, pockets are turned inside out.

items.example: I left my sunglasses in the car.
items.note: Plural noun; the illustrated exercise contrasts ordinary sunglasses with designer sunglasses.

sectionsChecked: A: Illustrated items of clothing, parts and plural-only forms
C: Clothing fit, style, materials and patterns

units.title: Unit 28 — Health and medicine
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 28. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.
learningObjectives: Recognise and accurately describe common symptoms, physical injuries and health problems.
Use correct collocations and prepositions, including have a sore throat, suffer a stroke, die of and recover from.
Distinguish informal and formal ways of discussing illness, such as pick up a bug, get over and recover from.
Describe common treatments using prescribe, take tablets, have an injection, wear a bandage, be in plaster and operate on.

items.example: A high temperature can be a symptom of an infection.
items.note: A change or problem felt by a person that may indicate illness.

items.example: He developed a rash after using the new soap.
items.note: An area of irritated skin, often red or itchy; common pattern: a rash on + body part.

items.example: She had a large bruise on her knee after the fall.
items.note: A coloured mark caused by an injury under the skin.

items.example: He asked a clinician about a small lump on his arm.
items.note: A swelling or raised area; the word itself does not establish a diagnosis.

items.example: She noticed several red spots on her neck.
items.note: Small marks on the skin; also means pimples in everyday British English.

items.pt: olho roxo; hematoma ao redor do olho
items.example: He had a black eye after an accidental collision in the game.
items.note: Bruising around the eye, usually following an impact.

items.example: I woke up with a sore throat and stayed home to rest.
items.note: Common collocation: have a sore throat.

items.example: She has a temperature and feels unusually tired.
items.note: British English commonly uses a temperature to mean a higher-than-normal body temperature; not merely having any temperature.

items.example: High blood pressure often needs regular monitoring.
items.note: Commonly called hypertension in medical contexts; not the same as heart disease.

items.example: The nurse checked whether he had low blood pressure.
items.note: Blood pressure lower than normal; medical term hypotension.

items.example: She sought urgent medical help because of chest pains.
items.note: Pain in the chest; the unit uses the plural expression chest pains.

items.example: I had backache after carrying heavy suitcases.
items.note: An aching pain in the back.

items.example: My nephew complained of earache during the flight.
items.note: A pain in the ear; contrast ear infection as a possible cause.

items.pt: uma dor na lateral do corpo
items.example: I noticed a pain in my side after the long run.
items.note: A usable first-person phrase from the source; side means the side of the torso.

items.example: Eating too quickly sometimes gives me indigestion.
items.note: Discomfort related to digestion; do not confuse with food poisoning.

items.example: The guests reported sickness and diarrhoea after the meal.
items.note: British sickness can mean vomiting; diarrhoea has British spelling and is uncountable here.

items.example: He had diarrhoea and needed to drink enough fluids.
items.note: British spelling diarrhoea; American diarrhea. Generally uncountable.

items.example: She got sunburn after forgetting to apply sunscreen.
items.note: Skin damage from too much exposure to the sun.

items.example: The doctor suspected a virus rather than a bacterial infection.
items.note: A virus is an infectious agent; not all symptoms have a viral cause.

items.example: My shoulders ache after moving all those boxes.
items.note: An ongoing dull pain; my back aches is a natural pattern.

items.example: My arms itch after walking through the tall grass.
items.note: The body part itches; a person scratches the area to relieve the feeling.

items.example: Try not to scratch the irritated skin.
items.note: The action you do because something itches; also means make a mark with nails.

items.example: His hands began to tremble after the frightening incident.
items.note: Shake slightly, sometimes because of fear or shock.

items.example: I started to shiver while waiting outside in the cold.
items.note: Often associated with cold or fever; different from tremble in emphasis.

items.example: My foot hurts where I hit it against the step.
items.note: Hurt can describe physical pain or mean cause injury; past form also hurt.

items.example: It took him a week to get over the infection.
items.note: Everyday phrasal verb meaning recover; also get over a cold or a bug.

items.example: She is still recovering from the flu.
items.note: More formal than get over; use recover from + illness, accident or injury.

items.example: She felt sick after the rough boat journey.
items.note: British English often means feel nauseous; American English can more broadly mean feel ill.

items.example: He was breathless after climbing several flights of stairs.
items.note: Unable to breathe normally for a short time or having difficulty breathing.

items.example: She felt dizzy when she stood up too quickly.
items.note: Feeling that you or your surroundings are spinning or that you may lose balance.

items.example: He said he had been feeling depressed for several weeks.
items.note: In everyday speech describes low mood; a clinical diagnosis requires professional assessment.

items.example: We were exhausted after the overnight journey.
items.note: Much more tired than simply tired.

items.example: She felt stressed about the upcoming deadline.
items.note: Feeling under pressure or strain.

items.example: He lost his appetite while he was unwell.
items.note: Appetite is the desire to eat; use lose + possessive + appetite.

items.pt: ficar sem voz; perder a voz
items.example: After the concert, she almost lost her voice.
items.note: To become temporarily unable to speak normally.

items.example: I think I picked up a bug during the trip.
items.note: Informal; a bug here means an infectious illness, not necessarily an insect.

items.pt: quebrar o pulso; fraturar o punho
items.example: He broke his wrist when he fell off his bicycle.
items.note: Break a bone is the everyday way to say fracture it; broken is the past participle.

items.example: She sprained her ankle while running on uneven ground.
items.note: A sprain involves injury to ligaments; distinct from a broken bone.

items.example: The player dislocated his shoulder during the match.
items.note: Dislocate means move a bone out of its normal joint position.

items.pt: morrer de (uma doença ou causa médica)
items.example: Her grandfather died of a heart attack many years ago.
items.note: In the source, die of is used with a heart attack; die from can also occur for some causes.

items.example: The family called an ambulance when they suspected a heart attack.
items.note: A serious medical emergency caused by interrupted blood flow to the heart.

items.example: Several passengers contracted an infection during the outbreak.
items.note: Formal verb for becoming infected. The source uses older wording about AIDS; in precise medical language a person contracts HIV, not AIDS.

items.pt: sofrer um AVC; ter um derrame
items.example: He suffered a stroke and required rehabilitation.
items.note: Formal phrase; informal equivalent: have a stroke.

items.example: The hospital has a specialist unit for patients recovering from a stroke.
items.note: A disruption of blood supply to part of the brain; also has unrelated meanings such as a movement.

items.example: The doctor prescribed a different medicine.
items.note: The medical verb for recommending or ordering a treatment; prescribe something for someone.

items.example: The label says to take a teaspoonful before bedtime.
items.note: Plural: teaspoonfuls; a measure of volume, not necessarily an ordinary household spoon.

items.example: The pharmacist explained how to take the medicine safely.
items.note: Uncountable when referring generally to a substance taken for treatment; can have specific countable uses.

items.example: A nurse put a bandage around his wrist.
items.note: A strip of material used to support or protect an injury.

items.example: They put a bandage on his ankle after checking the injury.
items.note: Collocation: put a bandage on + body part.

items.example: She needed an injection before travelling abroad.
items.note: A dose given with a needle; common pattern have an injection.

items.example: He had an injection at the clinic yesterday.
items.note: Natural collocation; British English commonly has have an injection.

items.example: The specialist said an operation might be necessary.
items.note: A surgical procedure; have an operation is a natural phrase.

items.example: She had an operation on her knee last year.
items.note: Patient-centred collocation for undergoing surgery.

items.example: His arm was in plaster for several weeks.
items.note: British English; American English often says in a cast.

items.example: The doctor decided to put the injured leg in plaster.
items.note: A passive form is also common: my leg was put in plaster.

items.example: The fracture took several weeks to mend.
items.note: Here mend describes a broken bone healing; also means repair objects.

items.example: The pharmacist told him when to take each tablet.
items.note: British English tablet; pill is also widely used in everyday speech.

items.example: She takes two tablets every evening as directed.
items.note: A natural treatment collocation; exact dosage must follow a professional's instructions.

items.example: The surgeon explained the planned procedure to the patient.
items.note: A medical professional who performs operations.

items.example: The surgical team operated on the patient in the morning.
items.note: Use operate on someone, not operate someone; key usage warning in the source.

items.example: The surgeon removed the tumour during the procedure.
items.note: British spelling tumour; American tumor; growth may be benign or malignant.

items.example: She saw a doctor about the ear infection.
items.note: Appears in the exercise dialogue as a possible explanation for earache.

items.example: The team organised a seminar about heart disease prevention.
items.note: Exercise vocabulary; general term covering several conditions affecting the heart.

items.example: The patient was referred to a psychiatrist for assessment.
items.note: Medical specialist mentioned in the matching exercise; not interchangeable with psychologist.

items.example: She reads for a few minutes at bedtime.
items.note: A useful time expression from the tablet-taking exercise.

sectionsChecked: A: Illustrated symptoms, signs, illness verbs and health-related adjectives
B: Medical prescriptions, treatment expressions and the operate on warning
